To tarnish something means to make it lose its shine, brightness, or clean appearance — either in a physical, literal sense (like metal going dull), or in a figurative sense (like a person's good reputation being damaged). Think of it as something that was once bright, clean, and admirable slowly becoming dull, dirty, or stained — not by being broken or destroyed, but by being spoiled.
Meaning 1 — The Literal, Physical Sense

When a shiny object, especially metal (like silver, brass, copper, or gold), is exposed to air, moisture, or certain chemicals over time, it gradually develops a dull, discoloured, dark film on its surface. That process is called tarnishing.

The object doesn't crack or fall apart. It still exists — but it no longer looks clean and bright. It looks dirty, spotted, or darkened.

Tarnish works in two directions here:

  • Something can tarnish on its own: "The silver spoons tarnished after being left in the drawer for years." (The spoons lost their shine by themselves, just from exposure to air.)
  • Something or someone can tarnish another thing: "The chemicals tarnished the silver bowl." (An outside force caused the shine to disappear.)

More examples:

  • "Her grandmother's necklace had tarnished to a dull grey."
  • "Leaving brass untreated will tarnish it quickly."
  • "The bronze statue had tarnished beautifully over the centuries, turning deep green."
Meaning 2 — The Figurative Sense (Far More Common in Everyday Use)

This is the meaning you will encounter most often. Here, tarnish means to damage, spoil, or stain someone's reputation, image, honour, or good name — or to spoil the quality or purity of something that was once admirable.

Just like metal loses its bright, clean appearance, a person, an organization, or even an achievement can lose its clean, respected image. It was once looked upon admirably — and now, because of some wrongdoing, scandal, lie, or bad behaviour, people no longer see it the same way.

Examples:

  • "The bribery scandal tarnished the politician's reputation." (His good name was damaged — people no longer respected him the way they once did.)
  • "One reckless act tarnished years of hard work." (All those years of effort were now seen in a negative light.)
  • "The team's victory was tarnished by allegations of cheating." (The win still happened, but it no longer felt clean or honourable.)
  • "She refused to let the lies tarnish her legacy." (She was protecting her good name from being spoiled.)
  • "His involvement in the scheme tarnished the company's image."

Notice something important: tarnish in this sense does not mean total destruction. The politician doesn't disappear; the victory doesn't get erased. Just like tarnished silver still exists, the person or achievement still exists — but the shine is gone. The clean, admirable quality is gone or reduced. This is what makes tarnish a precise and powerful word — it describes damage to image and honour, not complete elimination.
How the Two Meanings Connect

The figurative meaning grew naturally from the literal one. Both share the same core idea: something that was once bright, clean, and admirable becomes dull, stained, or spoiled — not by being destroyed, but by losing its clean quality. The physical image of a shiny silver spoon slowly going dark and dull is the perfect mental picture for what happens to a reputation when a scandal or dishonesty gets attached to it.
What Tarnish Is NOT

It's worth knowing what tarnish is not, so you don't confuse it with similar words.

  • Tarnish ≠ Destroy. To destroy something is to eliminate it entirely. To tarnish it is to spoil its quality or image while it still exists.
  • Tarnish ≠ Rust. Rust is specifically what happens to iron and steel. Tarnish typically refers to silver, brass, and copper — or figuratively, to reputations. (You would rarely say iron tarnishes; you'd say it rusts.)
  • Tarnish ≠ Criticise. Simply saying negative things about someone doesn't automatically tarnish them. Tarnish implies that the damage has actually stuck — that the reputation or image has genuinely been affected.
Who or What Can Be Tarnished?

In the figurative sense, here are the things most commonly tarnished:

  • Reputation — "The fraud tarnished his reputation permanently."
  • Image — "The incident tarnished the brand's image."
  • Legacy — "Nothing could tarnish the legacy of the great scientist."
  • Name / good name — "She worked hard so that no one could tarnish her name."
  • Record — "The doping scandal tarnished his otherwise clean record."
  • Honour / integrity — "He refused to do anything that would tarnish his integrity."
  • Achievement / victory / success — "The accusations tarnished what should have been a joyful win."
Synonyms — and How They Differ Slightly

For the figurative sense, words close in meaning include: sully, blemish, stain, smear, blacken, soil, taint, mar, damage.

  • Stain and tarnish are very close, but stain often suggests something more permanent and visible (like ink on cloth). Tarnish suggests a more gradual, dulling effect on something that was once shining.
  • Sully is slightly more formal and literary than tarnish.
  • Mar means to spoil or damage the appearance or quality of something — but it's broader and doesn't carry the specific "loss of shine" quality that tarnish does.
  • Taint often suggests contamination — as if something impure was introduced. Tarnish focuses more on the loss of a good image.

The closest, most interchangeable word is probably sully — but tarnish is far more commonly used and universally understood.
The Opposite of Tarnish

• Literally: to polish, shine, buff, clean, restore — bringing back the bright surface.
  • Figuratively: to restore, rehabilitate, burnish, protect, enhance — "Years of good work helped restore his tarnished reputation." (Notice you can say a reputation was tarnished and then later restored — showing again that tarnish is damage, not destruction.)
The Tone and Feel of the Word

Tarnish almost always carries a negative, slightly sorrowful tone. It suggests that something deserved to stay bright and clean — and it's a shame that it didn't. When someone says "That scandal tarnished his legacy," there's often an implied sadness: here was something admirable, and now it's been spoiled.

It's also a gradual-feeling word. Even though tarnish can happen from a single event, the word feels like something that creeps in slowly — the way metal darkens not all at once, but quietly, over time.
Quick Summary

To tarnish means to cause something shiny to become dull and discoloured (literally, as with metal), or to damage and spoil something admirable — especially a reputation, image, or legacy — so that it is no longer seen in a clean, respected light (figuratively). It describes damage to quality and appearance, not total destruction.
TAR-nish
